Thank you for submitting your article "Importance of miRNA stability and alternative primary miRNA isoforms in gene regulation during Drosophila development" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by Timothy Nilsen as Reviewing Editor and James Manley as the Senior Editor and three reviewers. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Hervé Seitz (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

This resubmitted manuscript is a significant improvement over the previous submission. The only remaining issue is the presentation of the 3D lineal model. Because this model is only presented in supplementary material, it is strongly suggested that the authors remove it from the manuscript. If they do so, the manuscript would be acceptable for eLife.

Reviewer #1:

In this new submission of a previously-reviewed manuscript, L. Zhou and colleagues quantify mature miRNAs and pri-miRNA precursors during Drosophila development, to derive molecular rules governing miRNA abundance in that dynamic process. The modified manuscript addresses most of my previous concerns, and it has been clearly improved. One of my main concerns remains though: the provided data suggest that the "3D lineal model" predicts mature miRNA abundance very poorly, most probably because of quantification inaccuracies (which may very well be impossible to improve with the current technologies). A precise description of that model is (still) desperately needed in the main text, as well as an estimation of the fitted coefficients' precision. The provided data suggest that precision is too low to permit the analyses that the authors perform – if so, then I would simply suggest to remove that modeling analysis (it would be mostly describing technical noise).

Once that issue is fixed, I think the manuscript will be a very good candidate for publication in eLife.

Essential revisions:

1) Regarding the "3D linear model" whose results are presented in Supplementary PDF 1: I appreciate the authors' clarification, but they mostly appear in their point-by-point response to the referees, and the readers themselves are left without much information. As I said in my evaluation of the first submission, it is important to write down the model's equation (please do that in the main text and write explicitly that the coefficient for "initial miRNA level" is expected to be negative, while the coefficient for "upstream density" is expected to be positive – and explain why, in each case). Without this, the reader will be completely lost. As for the accuracy of the estimation of coefficients by this model: the added sentence ("However, we note that this analysis has a caveat […]") is an improvement, but it lacks rigor. The fact that not every point falls on the plane is not a surprise (nothing is perfect in experimental science); the fact that they fall "far away" from the plane would be a problem, but for this we need to know how far is "far away". The authors' current formulation is deceiving ("significant" has a very precise meaning: it means that a statistical test was performed, and the null hypothesis was rejected with a given p-value cutoff). Here it looks like the authors use "significant" as a synonym for "large" (without defining how large is "large"), which it is not. Even more problematic, the fact that many slopes for "initial miRNA level" appear to be positive is not discussed. Honestly, from what I see, it looks like these measurements are extremely imprecise, and they cannot be used to conclude anything regarding the miRNA turnover rate. The fact that "5´ U" values end up begin mostly larger than "other 5´ nucleotide" values seems to be pure luck (with another, similarly imprecise RNA-Seq-based quantification, the values may have very well fallen in the opposite order). In their Point-by-point response, the authors say that the global analysis of every miRNA is certainly more precise than each individual measurement, which is certainly true – but whether this improvement is sufficient in order to perform an analysis like the one shown in Figure 6A remains to be demonstrated. For this, the authors need to evaluate the accuracy of their modeled coefficients (a linear modeling analysis does not only compute the fitted coefficients, it also provides an estimate of its precision; simply giving the coefficient without giving the precision is pointless). Given the aspect of the 3D graphs and given the dispersion of the points on Figure 6A (with the median for "5´ U" values being positive while their mean is negative), I expect precision to be too bad to allow a meaningful comparison of 5´ U miRNAs and 5´ non-U miRNAs (note that Figure 1D does not show that the model "worked reasonably well": most points fall next to the origin, with a high relative error). If indeed it is the case, then I recommend dropping the "3D linear model" analysis (which would be too noisy to be informative), and simply find another way to explain why the authors wanted to perform the analyses shown in Figure 6. (on a side note: Figure 6—figure supplement 1 is useless: if the authors wanted to compare 5´ U miRNAs to 5´ non-U miRNAs, they just had to compare the two datasets shown in Figure 6A, and they did not have to stratify "5´ non U" into "5´ A", "5´ C" and "5´ G" as shown in that supplement).

results.result: Small RNA composition changes during Drosophila embryogenesis, with category two small RNAs (endo-siRNA + piRNA) constituting >50% in 0-2hAEL embryos and declining until 12-18hAEL, while miRNA fraction increases concomitantly. In 18-24hAEL, rRNA-derived small RNAs increase without specific size peaks, suggesting they are degradation intermediates.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The compositional changes are clearly documented through small RNA library analysis with spike-in normalization. The interpretation of rRNA-derived small RNAs as degradation intermediates (C8) is appropriately presented as speculative.

results.result: Total mature miRNA abundance continuously increases throughout embryogenesis (8-fold from 0-2hAEL to 18-24hAEL), while piRNA population gradually decreases. These trends are consistent with expression patterns of miRNA and piRNA pathway components and with the notion that differentiated cells rely more on miRNA-mediated gene regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C14 are well-supported by spike-in normalized small RNA library data (Figure 1B) and mRNA expression data for pathway components (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The biological interpretation is appropriately supported by citations to previous literature and is consistent with the observed data.

results.result: Spike-in normalized small RNA library analysis accurately estimates miRNA expression levels relative to total RNA, as validated by Northern blotting. Total RNA per embryo remains relatively constant throughout embryogenesis, allowing library analysis to reflect relative abundance per embryo.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C18 are supported by comparison of library analysis with Northern blotting (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and measurement of total RNA per embryo (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A). The validation demonstrates the reliability of the spike-in normalization approach.

results.result: K-means clustering analysis groups miRNA genes into four clusters based on expression patterns. Cluster 1 (15 miRNAs) shows highest expression in early stages and consists mainly of maternally deposited miRNAs. Cluster 4 (6 genes) shows decrease in late stages, suggesting instability. The majority (75.8%, 66/87 genes) belong to clusters 2 and 3 showing increasing trends, indicating that increased miRNA abundance is a general trend not caused by a few species.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C27 are supported by k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 1C and are consistent with previous literature on maternal miRNA degradation (C20-C21) and miRNA stability (C23-C24). The statistical analysis appropriately characterizes the distribution of expression patterns across miRNA genes.

results.result: AGO1 protein levels are lower in very early embryos (0-2h and 2-4h), which may suggest AGO1 is a limiting factor for miRNA abundance or that lower miRNA levels trigger apo-AGO1 degradation.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 is supported by Western blot data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), but claims C29 and C30 are speculative interpretations. The correlation between AGO1 levels and miRNA abundance is noted but causality is not established. Alternative explanations are appropriately presented but not tested.

results.result: The large difference in total miRNA levels (8-fold increase from 0-2hAEL to 18-24hAEL) estimated by spike-in normalization underscores the importance of normalization method selection, as conventional RPM normalization disregards changes in small RNA population size.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by the observed data and comparison of normalization methods. The methodological point about RPM normalization is based on established knowledge (C32) and the spike-in approach provides a more accurate assessment of absolute abundance changes.

results.result: Pri-miRNAs have shorter half-lives than mature mRNAs or miRNAs. Transient peaks of pri-miRNA levels are often observed, suggesting miRNA transcription is activated in short time-windows. For clusters 2 and 3 miRNAs with highest mature levels in the last window, pri-miRNAs peak earlier while mature miRNA persists for hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 are supported by citations to previous literature (C33) and by data shown in Figure 1C. The observation of transient pri-miRNA peaks with persistent mature miRNA is consistent with the known stability differences between pri-miRNAs and mature miRNAs.

results.result: Multiple linear regression analysis based on two assumptions (transcription determines synthesis rate, degradation is proportional to miRNA abundance) accurately predicts miRNA change rates (r²=0.81). This suggests that for most miRNAs, production rate per pri-miRNA molecule and degradation rate remain relatively constant throughout embryogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 are supported by the regression analysis shown in Figure 1D. The model assumptions (C37-C38) are reasonable simplifications, and the high r² value (C39) supports the conclusion that these factors largely determine miRNA dynamics. However, the authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C48).

results.result: Predicted miRNA change rates tend to be higher than observed in early time windows, possibly due to less efficient processing, slower pri-miRNA degradation, or maternal miRNA effects. In other time windows, prediction errors show no clear trends, suggesting constant production/degradation kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C41 and C45 are supported by data in Figure 1E. Claims C42-C44 are appropriately presented as speculative explanations for the observed discrepancy. The analysis identifies a specific limitation of the model in early embryos while supporting the general conclusion for later stages.

results.result: Integrated analysis of mature and primary miRNAs confirms that transcription is important for determining mature miRNA expression patterns and suggests global miRNA production and degradation rates are relatively constant during embryogenesis except for early embryos. However, individual predictions may be inaccurate and some miRNAs may be regulated post-transcriptionally.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by the integrated analysis results. Claims C48-C49 appropriately acknowledge limitations and caveats. The overall conclusion is well-supported while recognizing that exceptions may exist and individual predictions have uncertainty.

results.result: The 5' nucleotide identity influences miRNA-Argonaute interactions, with 5'-U showing highest affinity. Regression analysis coefficients associated with mature miRNA abundance were generally higher for 5'-U miRNAs than others (p=0.01), suggesting 5'-U miRNAs may be more stable.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 is supported by citation (Frank et al., 2010) and C51 by established knowledge. However, C52 shows a statistically significant trend but the authors acknowledge many coefficients were unexpectedly positive, indicating inaccuracy in the analysis (as noted in text). Claim C53 is appropriately speculative. The computational analysis alone is insufficient to support the stability hypothesis.

results.result: Experimental validation shows that mutating 5'-A to 5'-U in miR-283 and two other miRNAs results in ~20% stabilization (p<0.02). Mutating to 5'-C also causes stabilization, while 5'-G mutation has no significant effect. The miR-283 star strand is present at very low levels, confirming measurements reflect mature miRNA half-lives in Argonaute complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 are well-supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-D and supplementary figures. The Northern blotting experiments with appropriate controls (C55) validate that the measurements reflect mature miRNA stability. The pattern of effects across different nucleotide substitutions (C56-C58) is consistent and statistically significant.

results.result: Analysis of 52 mature miRNAs from 13 clusters shows that while most cluster members show similar expression patterns (adjusted p>0.01), four clusters exhibit significant differences in at least one time window. This suggests some miRNAs are regulated by additional mechanisms beyond transcriptional control.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 are supported by data in Figure 4 and statistical analysis (Supplementary file 5). The expectation of co-regulation (C60-C61) is based on established knowledge, and the observation of exceptions (C62, C65) is well-documented. The inference about additional regulatory mechanisms (C66) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: The mir-317 cluster consists of three miRNAs with roles in aging. Five major pri-miRNA isoforms with alternative TSSs and TTSs were identified, including a short isoform covering only mir-277. This short isoform is the main form in embryos with peak expression at 14-18hAEL, coinciding with the time window showing significant differences between miR-277 and miR-317/-34 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 are supported by citations to previous literature. Claims C70-C73 are supported by data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The identification of alternative isoforms and their correlation with differential expression patterns provides a mechanistic explanation for the observed cluster member differences.

results.result: Adult tissues use long pri-mir-317 isoforms as the main form, with higher relative levels of miR-317/-34 compared to miR-277 than in embryos. Histone modification changes at alternative TSS sites support the alternative TSS hypothesis. The authors favor the hypothesis that alternative TSS/TTS selection alters relative miRNA levels, though processing intermediates are not formally excluded.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 are supported by data in Figure 5A and supplementary figures. Claim C77 is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). Claim C76 is appropriately speculative. Claim C78 represents the authors' interpretation while acknowledging alternative explanations, which is appropriate given the supporting evidence.

results.result: The mir-317 cluster is controlled by ecdysone. In Kc167 cells, 20-HE treatment selectively down-regulates long transcripts (TSS1/2), causing stronger decrease of miR-317/-34 than miR-277. Similar trends occur in S2-R+ cells. BG3-c2 cells express only long isoforms and show similar decrease of all three miRNAs upon 20-HE treatment. These results validate that transcriptional control through multiple promoters enables differential regulation within clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C88 are well-supported by data in Figure 5B-C and supplementary figures. The cell culture experiments with ecdysone treatment provide direct evidence for differential regulation of pri-miRNA isoforms and resulting effects on mature miRNA levels. The validation across multiple cell lines strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: The mir-309 cluster is transcribed transiently in very early embryos and is essential for maternal-to-zygotic transition, though individual miRNA roles are not well understood. After 2-4hAEL, the decrease rate of mature miRNA levels reflects degradation rates since there is no evidence for new synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by citations to previous literature and by RNA-seq data (Figure 6A). Claim C93 is a reasonable assumption based on the lack of pri-miRNA expression after 2-4hAEL. This assumption is critical for the subsequent half-life analysis.

results.result: mir-309 cluster miRNAs exhibit distinct degradation rates. K-means clustering divides them into two groups: miR-3/miR-309 (fast) and miR-4/-5/-6/-286 (slow). miR-3/-309 show 3-10 times faster degradation rates. Northern blotting confirms the faster disappearance, excluding sequencing artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 are well-supported by data in Figure 4, Figure 6B-D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The clustering analysis appropriately groups miRNAs by degradation kinetics, and the Northern blotting validation (C97) excludes technical artifacts as an explanation.

results.result: AGO1 immunoprecipitation experiments show no obvious difference in loading efficiency between stable and unstable mir-309 cluster miRNAs. Clear reduction of mature miRNAs in supernatant indicates a large fraction are properly loaded to AGO1. Therefore, the difference in reduction rates reflects differences in mature miRNA stability within the Argonaute complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by data in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2. The AGO1-IP experiments appropriately test and exclude the alternative hypothesis that differential loading efficiency explains the observed differences. The conclusion that stability differences occur within Argonaute complexes is well-supported.

results.result: Reanalysis of D. virilis small RNA library data reveals similar trends in relative half-lives of orthologous mir-309 cluster miRNAs, suggesting rapid down-regulation of miR-3/-309 has evolutionarily conserved roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are supported by reanalysis of published data (Ninova et al., 2014) shown in Figure 6B. The conservation of differential degradation rates across species supports the biological importance of this regulatory mechanism. However, the analysis uses different normalization methods (TMM vs spike-in) which could introduce some uncertainty.

results.result: miR-3 and miR-309 share the same seed sequence and regulate overlapping target sets. A genome-wide overexpression screen showed miR-3 overexpression causes embryonic/early larval lethality, while other cluster members do not when individually overexpressed.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 is supported by sequence data (Figure 7A) and citation to Bartel, 2009. Claim C104 is appropriately speculative. Claims C105-C106 are supported by citation to Bejarano et al., 2012. These observations provide context for investigating the biological importance of rapid miR-3/-309 degradation.

results.result: Embryos overexpressing miR-3/-309 exhibit denticle organization defects, a phenotype associated with planar cell polarity (PCP) defects. Misexpression of miR-3 in the developing notum causes bristle misorientation, demonstrating biological activity in PCP in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by data in Figure 7B-C. The denticle phenotype (C107) and bristle misorientation (C109) are well-documented. The inference about PCP defects (C108) is supported by citation to Donoughe and DiNardo, 2011 and is consistent with the observed phenotypes.

results.result: Vang encodes a transmembrane protein integral to the Frizzled-mediated PCP pathway. Luciferase sensor assays show Vang 3'UTR expression is significantly repressed by miR-3 co-overexpression, and this repression depends on predicted target sites. These results verify Vang 3'UTR is a bona fide target of miR-3.
results.evaluation: Claim C110 is supported by citations to previous literature. Claims C111-C113 are well-supported by luciferase sensor data in Figure 7D. The site-directed mutagenesis control (C112) appropriately demonstrates specificity of the miRNA-target interaction.

results.result: Vang mRNA is up-regulated in mir-309 cluster null mutants and down-regulated upon miR-3/-309 overexpression in mixed stage embryos. In late stage embryos where miR-3/-309 are undetectable, Vang expression is not significantly altered in mutants but can be repressed by overexpression. Overexpressed miR-3/-309 levels do not exceed natural peak levels, confirming physiological relevance.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C118 are well-supported by data in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The stage-specific effects (C115-C116) are consistent with the rapid degradation of miR-3/-309 and support the biological importance of this regulation. The verification of physiological expression levels (C117-C118) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Reanalysis of RNA-seq data shows the reduction of miR-3/-309 precedes the increase of Vang mRNA, consistent with the hypothesis that rapid degradation of miR-3/-309 is biologically important. Taken together, observations support this notion.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by reanalysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2. The temporal relationship between miRNA decrease and target mRNA increase is consistent with the proposed regulatory mechanism. The overall conclusion (C120) is well-supported by the combined experimental and computational evidence.

results.result: 3'UTRs tend to avoid seed target sequences of co-expressed miRNAs, leaving evolutionary signatures detectable by population genetics.
